title: I overpaid for one unit and another was abandoned. Should I sell?
excerpt: A 31-year-old owns a Mont Kiara unit bought at the peak, a once-abandoned studio in Selayang and a new home that stretches her budget. Sean says hold both investments for now and get the numbers first.

question.asker: From Miss E, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Miss E and her husband are 31. At 24 they bought a 494 sq ft commercial-titled unit in Mont Kiara for RM560,000, about RM1,200 psf, where listings now ask RM700 to RM900 psf; the 25-year loan costs about RM3,000 a month and it rents for RM1,700 to RM1,900. She also co-owns a studio in Selayang with her brother, bought in 2014 with their parents paying the down payment; the project was abandoned, is now being completed by a new developer, and they have kept paying the loan. Last year the couple bought their own home, and money now feels tight.
question.text: Should she sell the Mont Kiara unit or keep renting it out, and should she sell the Selayang studio once she gets the keys or rent it out?

answer.quote: It's just very dangerous to buy a particular location at its peak price.
answer.summary: Hold both for now. For the Mont Kiara unit, find out what she still owes the bank and test short-term rental, since the area is picking up. For the Selayang studio, wait until the keys are handed over, then decide from real rents, prices and what is left on the loan.

reasons.title: Selling below the loan still leaves a debt
reasons.body: If she owes the bank RM500,000 and sells for RM450,000, she loses the unit and still has to pay the RM50,000 difference. Knowing the outstanding loan comes before any decision to sell.

reasons.title: Short stays may beat a long-term tenant
reasons.body: The building feels like a hotel and short-stay rates have recovered since Covid. Run it herself, which is close to a full-time job, or partner with an operator on a profit split, and compare the result with RM1,700 to RM1,900 a month.

reasons.title: Mont Kiara is picking up
reasons.body: New completions, a mixed development, more launches and a possible MRT line nearby should bring more people. Holding is about reducing her loss rather than counting on big gains.

reasons.title: Banks still collect on abandoned projects
reasons.body: Buyers must repay what the bank has already released to the developer, even with no home to move into. Standard billing schedules for developers only limit the damage, and a revived project is close to a miracle, so the next step is to see it completed.

actions: Ask the bank exactly how much is still owed on each property.
Check daily and weekend short-stay rates in the Mont Kiara building and talk to operators there.
Hold the Selayang studio until vacant possession, then check its rent, latest selling prices and the mall's anchor tenants.
Before any future purchase, compare the price per square foot with the area's median price.
Look at price per square foot, not just the total price, when a unit seems affordable.
caveat: Sean doubts the Selayang location, where few projects have done well, so the decision on that studio may change once the real rents and prices are known. With three incomes sharing the loans and her age on her side, he sees the situation as fixable rather than the end of the world.
sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #206. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer stated them in March 2023.
